CHAPTER 8: SOCIAL CLASS AND GENDER

LEARNING OUTCOME 2.3: SOCIAL CLASS AND GENDER AS IMPORTANT SOCIAL CATEGORIES
- Evaluate what is meant by 'social class'.
- Illustrate and critically evaluate the view that in capitalism, social class is an important way of categorising who has and has not got power.
- Discuss what is meant by 'patriarchy'.
- Illustrate the view that in a patriarchy, gender is an important way of categorising who has power; critically evaluate the view that modern Irish society is a patriarchy.

8.1 SOCIAL CLASS AS A SOCIAL CATEGORY
MARGINALISATION
- Marginalisation: treating a person, group or concept as insignificant or peripheral. Caused by direct or indirect discrimination, or by implicit bias.
- Implicit bias: unconscious attitudes, beliefs or stereotypes people hold towards groups or individuals without being aware of them.
- Marginalised groups in Ireland: Travelling community, women, the working class, people with disabilities, LGBTQ+ community. Internationally: Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar, Uighur Muslims in China, women in places like Iran and Afghanistan.

SOCIAL STRATIFICATION AND CLASS
- Social stratification: division of society into layers (strata) - a hierarchy of social groups with advantage or disadvantage in income, wealth, occupation, race or sex. Those at the top usually have more power. Sociologists say some form exists in every society.
- Social class: a group of people who share the same socio-economic status.
- Capitalism: an economic system where private individuals or businesses own and operate the means of production, distribution and exchange; driven by profit, with minimal government interference.
- Social conflict theory: individuals and groups interact on the basis of conflict; society is unequal and needs change; powerful groups exploit the powerless. Marx and Engels: all of human history is the result of class conflict.
- How stratification occurs: 1. Economic privilege (more access to money/resources); 2. Social prestige (personal or social qualities valued more highly); 3. Power (access to more powerful positions).
- Privilege activity: examples include never sharing a bedroom, owning a second home, private health insurance, parents who went to university, private school, never skipping meals for lack of money, connections for jobs (e.g. TY work experience). Privilege is subjective.

KARL MARX (1818-1883) - KEY THINKER
- German philosopher, economist and political theorist; critic of capitalism; key to socialist and communist theory. Works: The Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital.
- Quote: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways. The point, however, is to change it.'
- Communist theory: aims for a classless society where wealth and resources are shared equally.
- Capitalism is exploitative and causes inequality and alienation.
- Alienation: feeling disconnected from something important. Under capitalism people are alienated from their labour, the products they make, other people and their own human nature.
- Communism: workers collectively own and control the means of production; working class must overthrow the capitalist class and set up socialism. Principle: 'from each according to their ability, to each according to their needs'. No private property or classes.
- Means of production: resources, tools and infrastructure needed to produce goods and services - factories, machinery, raw materials, labour power.
- Class struggle: history is conflict between classes. Bourgeoisie (capitalist class) own the means of production; proletariat (working class) only have their labour to sell.
- Profit exploitation: capitalists pay workers as little as possible to maximise profit. Workers try to get higher wages and better conditions (labour as a commodity).
- Workers have no say in how work is organised - alienated from their labour; competition for jobs isolates workers from each other.
- False consciousness: workers may not even realise they are being exploited.
- Class consciousness: workers becoming aware of their oppression - Marx expected this to lead to revolution.
- Communist Manifesto: 'Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains!'

PIERRE BOURDIEU AND CAPITAL
- French sociologist, 1970s: social class depends not only on economic resources but on non-economic resources (capital) that allow social mobility.
- Economic capital: money and property.
- Social capital: connections with friends, family, colleagues; resources from networks and group membership that give power in the social hierarchy - a social advantage.
- Cultural capital: knowledge, skills, education; knowing how the world works - recognising references in books and media, how to act (table manners), speech, accent, dress.
- Middle-class parents give children linguistic and cultural skills that help them succeed in school and university; working-class children without these are less successful. So education reproduces class inequality. Economic and cultural capital reinforce each other: success leads to better-paid jobs, which buy private education for the next generation (source: A Dictionary of Sociology, Oxford Reference).
- Social mobility: ability to move from one social class to another; e.g. education can empower lower classes.

IS IRELAND A CLASS-BASED SOCIETY? (consider income, housing, healthcare, education)
CASE STUDY: HOUSING CRISIS
- CSO: in the year to January 2023, average house price in Dublin over €430,000 vs national average around €305,000.
- Hardest hit: people on low incomes or with less social capital - low wages, insecure/part-time work, people with disabilities or mental health issues.
- Over 11,000 people homeless in 2023, over 3,000 of them children (Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage).
- Critics: lack of social housing and reliance on private rental - in 2021 over 25% of households rented privately (CSO), bringing insecure tenure, poor quality and unaffordable rents.
- Housing for All plan (2022) schemes: First Home Scheme (helps first-time buyers buy new homes); Local Authority Home Loan (borrow up to 90% of market value); cost rental homes with rents at least 25% below market; Help to Buy extended to end of 2024 (helped over 35,000 buy first homes by late 2022); Housing First National Implementation Plan 2022-26 - 1,319 new supported tenancies for long-term homeless with complex needs (680 in Housing First tenancies by end of 2021).
- Taoiseach Micheál Martin: difficulties from war in Ukraine, energy crisis and rising interest rates; updated plan focuses on delivering homes 'at scale and speed'. Critics say root causes are not addressed.
- Winter of Housing Discontent protest, Dublin 2021, organised by the National Homeless and Housing Coalition.
- Egalitarianism: belief that all people are equal and deserve equal rights and opportunities.

CASE STUDY: EFFORTS TO REDUCE SOCIO-ECONOMIC INEQUALITY
- Minimum wage: €11.30 per hour in January 2023 (Citizens Information); one of the highest in the EU (Eurostat). A living wage to replace it from 2026, set at 60% of median wage. Argued to reduce income inequality.
- Living wage: minimum income needed to meet basic needs and a reasonable standard of living (housing, food, healthcare, transport etc.).
- Tax system: 2020 ESRI study - no tax system in Europe does more to reduce household income inequality. Before taxes and benefits, Ireland has the most unequal income distribution in the EU; progressive tax brings take-home inequality close to the EU average. Dr Barra Roantree: key features are the broad-based Universal Social Charge and the early point at which the higher rate of income tax starts.
- Welfare system: Social Justice Ireland (2022) - the key to reducing inequality; supports unemployed, disabled and those in hardship, plus healthcare, housing help, education and training. CSO 2022: without social welfare almost four in ten people would be in poverty.
- Social protection spending: EU-27 average per inhabitant €8,416 (2019) rose over 8% to €9,105 (2020), largest rise in 10 years (Covid-19). Ireland spent €11,348 per person in 2021 (up from €11,213 in 2020); 10th in EU.

OTHER THINKERS ON SOCIAL CLASS
- Paulo Freire: education as a tool to challenge social inequality; raise awareness (consciousness) among marginalised and working-class groups so they can fight oppression; students reflect critically on how society shaped their lives.
- John Rawls (additional thinker): a just society gives equal opportunity regardless of class; rejected rewards based solely on merit; advantages should benefit the least advantaged; class shaped by social and cultural factors too; inequalities justified only if they help the least well off.
- Robert Nozick: minimal state; rejects intervention; distribution of wealth is a matter of individual choice and free exchange, not justice. Critics: ignores structural inequalities (education, healthcare), so class decides opportunities.
- Also link: Kathleen Lynch (equality of condition), Martha Nussbaum (capabilities), right to housing, SDGs.

8.2 GENDER AS A SOCIAL CATEGORY
- Patriarchy: a system of society or government in which men hold most power and resources, marginalising women and other gender minorities.
- Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949): 'Her wings are cut and then she is blamed for not knowing how to fly.'
- Debate points: gender roles, pay gap, gender-based violence, under-representation in leadership, women's role in the home, gender-segregated schools.

SYLVIA WALBY (born 1953) - KEY THINKER
- Feminist scholar; studies how gender intersects with race, class and sexuality.
- Private patriarchy: patriarchal power within the family and relationships - control and exploitation of women's labour, sexuality and reproduction. Linked to capitalism, which relies on women's unpaid domestic labour (cooking, cleaning, childcare) to maintain the workforce, allowing men to do paid work.
- Unpaid labour: work not recognised or paid in the formal economy, e.g. caring and household chores.
- Public patriarchy: patriarchal power embedded in wider social, economic and political structures - legal system, labour markets, education, politics - which exclude or disadvantage women and privilege men.
- SIX STRUCTURES OF PATRIARCHY:
- 1. Household: women do most domestic and care work; unpaid labour is invisible and undervalued.
- 2. Paid work: women paid less for the same work; concentrated in low-paid, low-status jobs; under-represented in leadership.
- 3. The state: women under-represented in politics and decision-making; women's issues underfunded.
- 4. Male violence against women: domestic and sexual violence, harassment; victims blamed; systemic because states that only condemn it perpetuate it by non-interference.
- 5. Sexuality: objectification; women's sexuality controlled and policed; women shamed while men's behaviour normalised.
- 6. Cultural institutions: women under-represented in media, arts, sport, literature; contributions ignored; media portrays women in sexualised ways, creating stereotypes.
- Walby quote: 'Liberated from the home, women now have the whole of society in which to be exploited.'

FEMINISM
- Feminism: a social, political and cultural movement for gender equality that works to dismantle patriarchy and gender-based oppression.
- bell hooks, Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center - feminism is a movement to end sexism, sexist exploitation and oppression; it is anti-patriarchal and cannot ignore racism, classism, homophobia.
- Intersectionality: term coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 - forms of oppression (racism, sexism, homophobia, classism) interact, creating unique experiences for people with multiple marginalised identities.
- First wave (late 19th - early 20th century, US and Europe): suffrage (vote), property rights, education; Suffragettes Emmeline Pankhurst and Hannah Sheehy-Skeffington.
- Second wave (1960s-70s): reproductive rights, workplace discrimination, sexuality; more radical; consciousness-raising; experiences of women of colour. Example: 1971 women took the train from Connolly Station to Belfast to buy contraceptives, illegal in the Republic.
- Third wave (1990s): gender identity, LGBTQ+ rights, globalisation, indigenous rights, technology; inclusivity. 2018: 8th Amendment repealed 66.4% to 33.6%, over two million votes, 64.5% turnout.
- Possible fourth wave: social media, gender quotas, #MeToo, sexual harassment and gender-based violence debates, 'equalist' movement.
- Feminism's achievements: voting rights, awareness of sexual harassment and gender-based violence, debate on gender roles, workplace equality.
- TYPES OF FEMINISM:
- Liberal (first wave): legal and political systems are the main source of inequality; fix through legal reform and policy.
- Radical (second wave): dismantle patriarchal power; focus on sexuality, reproductive rights, violence against women.
- Marxist (second wave): gender oppression comes from the economic system where women's labour is devalued and unpaid; challenge capitalism.
- Ecofeminism (second wave): links exploitation of women and exploitation of nature (link Vandana Shiva).
- Black feminism (second wave): race, gender and class intersect to create distinct oppression; challenges erasure of black women.
- Intersectional (third wave): inclusive; challenges a feminism centred on white, middle-class, cisgender Western women.
- Nuance: subtle differences within a situation or idea that need careful analysis.

CASE STUDY: IS GENDER A SOCIAL CONSTRUCT?
- Are there social expectations by gender? Women expected to be caring, emotional homemakers; men strong, unemotional breadwinners.
- Kathleen Lynch: Ireland traditionally stressed women as carers/homemakers and men as breadwinners.
- Women earned 14.4% less than men on average in 2020 (Eurostat/CSO).
- Women in the Dáil: 16.3% to 22.2% after 2016; little change after 2020. EU average rose from 27.7% to 31.2% (2014-2018); Ireland tenth lowest in the EU.
- Women's Aid (2021): one in four women in Ireland who have been in a relationship experienced domestic violence.
- Men: pressure to be strong, dominant, competitive. CSO (2022): men were 76% of deaths by suicide in 2019. Road Safety Authority (2023): men were 78% of drivers in fatal collisions in 2022.

CASE STUDY: IS THERE A GENDER PAY GAP?
- Gender pay gap: difference in average gross hourly earnings between women and men (before tax and social security).
- Ireland: women earned 14.4% less in 2020, gap larger in higher-paid jobs.
- Causes (European Parliament): part-time and unpaid work - 28% of women vs 8% of men work part-time in the EU (Eurostat 2020); career breaks - in 2018 a third of employed women had a work interruption for childcare vs 1.3% of men; fewer female managers - 34% of EU managers in 2020 though almost half of employees; female managers earn 23% less per hour than male managers.
- Gap grows with age; gender pension gap over 28% in the EU in 2020 - women at greater risk of poverty in old age.
- December 2022: EU agreed companies must disclose pay information to expose gaps.
- Equal Pay Day 2023 in Ireland: 21 November (European Commission). EU-wide figure: women paid 14.1% less per hour, almost two months' salary.
- Counter-arguments: gap due to choices (time off for children, lower-paid professions, fewer hours) or differences in qualifications/experience, not discrimination. A 'motherhood pay gap': OECD found women earn 22% less on average, 33% less for women with children - so cheaper childcare is needed. Forbes (2016) 'Don't Buy Into the Gender Pay Gap Myth' called it statistical manipulation. Claudia Goldin (Harvard, 2016, 'Reassessing the Gender Wage Gap'): women seek flexibility, leading to part-time, lower-paid jobs; men reach higher corporate positions.
- Gender quota: policy requiring a percentage of positions to be held by a particular gender to address under-representation (politics, boards, institutions). Link to positive discrimination.

KATHLEEN LYNCH - AFFECTIVE INEQUALITY (KEY THINKER)
- Unequal distribution of care and emotional labour; care work (e.g. childcare) is unpaid or undervalued and mostly done by women.
- Overlooked because emotional labour is seen as 'natural' or 'instinctive' rather than work deserving pay.
- Care commanders: people with power and resources to direct care (policymakers, employers) - usually men. Footsoldiers: people who do care work (nurses, teachers, childcare workers) - usually women.
- CSO census 2016: 4.1% of population (195,263 people) are unpaid carers; over 60% women; worth €10 billion a year to the State.

MARTHA NUSSBAUM - CAPABILITIES APPROACH (KEY THINKER)
- Universal set of basic capabilities everyone needs for a dignified life; focus on what people can do and achieve, not just resources.
- Gender justice: a 'social minimum' of capabilities for all, including women - healthy life, political participation, freedom of expression, education, basic economic resources - giving equality and autonomy.
- Example: 2022 Irish parental leave increased to seven weeks' paid leave for both parents, promoting shared caring and women's participation at work.

EXAM POINTS
- HL essays: 'Low socio-economic status, not gender, is the greatest barrier to power in a capitalist society' (2020); Walby's 'Liberated from the home...'; Varadkar March 2023 on Article 41.2 (woman's place in the home) - result of patriarchy?; in capitalism is class a way of categorising power?; is contemporary Ireland a patriarchy (2022); gender pay gap complex issue (2021).
- Essay intro structure: main arguments (MA), Key Thinkers (KT), data analysis (DA), counter-argument.
- HL short: thinker who sees tax as theft (Nozick); philosophy minimising government (libertarianism); thinker on carers (Lynch).

rows.prompt: Explain what Marx meant by alienation.
rows.model_answer: Alienation is feeling disconnected from something important. Marx said that under capitalism workers are alienated from their labour and the products they make because capitalists own the means of production and workers have no say. They are also alienated from each other through competition, and from their own human nature.

rows.prompt: Explain Marx's theory of class struggle.
rows.model_answer: Marx believed all history is conflict between classes. Under capitalism the bourgeoisie own the means of production and the proletariat only have their labour to sell; capitalists pay as little as possible to maximise profit (profit exploitation). Marx expected workers to develop class consciousness and overthrow the capitalist class, creating a classless communist society.

rows.prompt: Name and explain Bourdieu's three forms of capital.
rows.model_answer: Economic capital is money and property. Social capital is the connections with family, friends and colleagues that give advantage. Cultural capital is knowledge, skills, education and ways of speaking, dressing and behaving that help people navigate the world.

rows.prompt: Describe two schemes in the Housing for All plan (2022).
rows.model_answer: The Help to Buy scheme was extended to the end of 2024 and had helped over 35,000 people buy their first home by late 2022. The Local Authority Home Loan lets applicants borrow up to 90% of a property's value. Cost rental homes have rents at least 25% below the private market.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a minimum wage and a living wage.
rows.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay set by law; in Ireland it was €11.30 in January 2023. A living wage is the minimum income needed to meet basic needs like housing, food and healthcare and have a reasonable standard of living. Ireland's living wage is to be set at 60% of the median wage from 2026.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between Walby's private and public patriarchy.
rows.model_answer: Private patriarchy is power exercised within the family, especially through women's unpaid domestic labour, sexuality and reproduction, which supports capitalism. Public patriarchy is power built into wider structures such as the legal system, labour markets, education and politics, which exclude or disadvantage women.

rows.prompt: Describe the three waves of feminism.
rows.model_answer: The first wave (late 19th-early 20th century) fought for the vote, property rights and education, led by suffragettes like Hannah Sheehy-Skeffington. The second wave (1960s-70s) focused on reproductive rights, workplace discrimination and sexuality. The third wave (1990s) focused on gender identity, LGBTQ+ rights, globalisation and inclusivity.

rows.prompt: Give two causes of the gender pay gap from the chapter.
rows.model_answer: Women do more unpaid work and part-time work: 28% of EU women work part-time compared with 8% of men. Women take more career breaks for childcare (a third of employed women in 2018 vs 1.3% of men), and there are fewer female managers (34%), who earn 23% less per hour than male managers.

rows.prompt: Explain Kathleen Lynch's theory of affective inequality.
rows.model_answer: Affective inequality is the unequal distribution of care and emotional labour. Care work like childcare is mostly done by women and is unpaid or undervalued because it is seen as 'natural'. Care commanders who direct care are usually men, while footsoldiers who do it are usually women.

rows.prompt:
Study the data below and answer the question.

'Women in Ireland earned 14.4% less than men in 2020. In the EU, 28% of women work part-time compared to 8% of men. In 2018, a third of employed women had a work interruption for childcare, compared to 1.3% of men. Women make up 34% of managers and female managers earn 23% less per hour than male managers.'

What does this data suggest about the causes of the gender pay gap? (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The data suggests the gender pay gap of 14.4% is linked to caring responsibilities. Far more women (28%) than men (8%) work part-time, which pays less, often because women do more unpaid care work. A third of employed women took career breaks for childcare compared to only 1.3% of men, which slows their career progress. Women are also under-represented in senior roles, at 34% of managers, and even female managers earn 23% less per hour. This supports Walby's view of patriarchal relations in paid work, although some argue it reflects choices or a 'motherhood pay gap' rather than discrimination.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 points x 2.5 marks, each linked to the data: part-time work gap (28% v 8%); career breaks for childcare (a third v 1.3%); fewer women managers (34%); female managers earn 23% less; overall gap 14.4%; link to unpaid care/patriarchy or counter-view (choices, motherhood gap).

rows.prompt: Explain how Pierre Bourdieu's ideas on capital help us understand social class in Ireland. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Bourdieu argued class is shaped not only by economic capital (money and property) but by social and cultural capital. Social capital is connections with family, friends and colleagues; for example, some young people get good jobs or work experience through family connections. Cultural capital is knowledge, education, accent and manners. Middle-class parents pass these on, so their children do better at school and university, while working-class children without them are less successful. In this way education reproduces class inequality. Economic and cultural capital reinforce each other: well-paid jobs let families buy private education, keeping advantage within the same class. In Ireland, people with less social capital also struggle more with housing, where Dublin prices were over €430,000.
rows.marking_scheme: Explanation of Bourdieu's forms of capital: 4 marks (economic, social, cultural, 1-2 marks each up to 4). Application to Ireland / class reproduction: 6 marks (3 points x 2 marks), e.g. education reproduces inequality, connections for jobs, capitals reinforce each other, housing and social capital.

rows.prompt: 'Modern Irish society is a patriarchy.' Discuss, with reference to at least two thinkers you have studied. (60 marks)
rows.model_answer:
I agree that modern Irish society is still a patriarchy, although real progress has been made. Patriarchy is a system in which men hold most power and resources, marginalising women. Sylvia Walby's six structures of patriarchy and Kathleen Lynch's theory of affective inequality show that it remains in both private and public life.

First, private patriarchy remains in the household. Walby argues women do most unpaid domestic and care work, which supports the capitalist economy. Irish data supports this: over 60% of the 195,263 unpaid carers in the 2016 census were women, doing work worth €10 billion a year. Lynch explains that this care is undervalued because it is seen as 'natural', and that care commanders are usually men while footsoldiers are usually women.

Second, public patriarchy is clear in paid work and the state. Women in Ireland earned 14.4% less than men in 2020. Only 34% of EU managers are women and female managers earn 23% less per hour. In politics, women made up only 22.2% of the Dáil after 2016, little changed after 2020, leaving Ireland tenth lowest in the EU.

Third, male violence against women continues. Women's Aid found one in four women who have been in a relationship experienced domestic violence. Walby argues this is systemic when states only condemn it.

However, there are counter-arguments. Feminist waves have brought change: women can vote, the 8th Amendment was repealed in 2018 by 66.4% to 33.6%, and parental leave rose to seven weeks' paid leave in 2022, which Martha Nussbaum would see as building a 'social minimum' of capabilities. Some argue the pay gap reflects choices or a 'motherhood pay gap', as Claudia Goldin suggests. Patriarchy also harms men: men were 76% of suicides in 2019 and 78% of drivers in fatal collisions in 2022, showing rigid gender norms affect everyone.

Overall, while laws have changed, the evidence on care, pay, representation and violence shows that patriarchal structures remain in Ireland today.
